vignette:
Ravi Patel is a 68-year-old South Asian American man who came to treatment months after being raped in a building where he had been staying overnight for work with the nonprofit that employs him. He has found it almost impossible to describe the assault directly. In the first sessions he circled around it, saying he knew exactly what happened but could not find words for it, as if language stopped where the worst part began. What comes back most clearly are sounds and sensations: a footstep in the hallway, the shift of a door, the attacker’s breathing, and the pain in his body in the same places that were hurt that night. Those fragments make ordinary noises feel charged. Even now, if he hears an unexpected sound in his apartment or in the office after hours, his body reacts as though someone may be entering.

In the weeks afterward, Ravi had come to believe that the way he was reacting meant something shameful about him. He was certain that a stronger man would have coped better, spoken more clearly, and moved on. He told himself that since the assault he was a lousy coper, permanently changed, cut off from the ordinary emotional life other people seemed to have. As a divorced older man who already felt somewhat separate from younger coworkers, he began to experience himself as an outsider in a more final way, as though the assault had pushed him beyond the edge of ordinary human belonging. These conclusions did not stay abstract. The more he judged himself as broken and permanently different, the more he watched for danger, listening for signs of intrusion at home and remaining on high alert around sudden sounds, convinced that his world was no longer basically safe.

That same self-judgment also shaped what he did to get through the day. Ravi began arranging himself against walls in conference rooms, waiting areas, and even at staff lunches so that no one could come up behind him. When the sense of danger was this constant, these precautions felt to Ravi less like choices than like the only way to get through the day; staying near exits, avoiding empty rooms, and sometimes hurting himself to break the surge of alarm were all attempts to make the threat feel briefly more manageable. At the nonprofit office, if a meeting room filled before he could choose the chair he wanted, he would hover near the door or find a reason not to stay. He increasingly avoided being alone in a room or a building, especially near closing time, because being alone with his own reactions felt intolerable and, to him, further proof that he could not manage what had happened. On his worst evenings, overwhelmed and disgusted with himself for still being so affected, he hurt himself physically to release the pressure, a private act he described less as wanting to die than as needing a sharp sensation that cut through the emotional flooding.

The memories themselves tightened this pattern. When the assault returned, it did not feel like a distant recollection. What made them seize him so forcefully was often the way he had come to think about himself since the rape: when he told himself that a stronger man would have fought, spoken, or recovered differently, the scene came back with punishing clarity, as if his mind kept reopening it to show him evidence of his weakness and damage. He heard the sounds in his head and felt pain in his body, and those episodes left him desperate not to be by himself with what might come next. After nights when he lay awake listening for any sound that might mean someone was entering his home, he would call a colleague just to keep another voice on the line. The memories also deepened his conviction that something in him had been permanently altered. Each time he could not put the experience into words, he took that as evidence not simply of distress but of damage: proof, in his mind, that he had lost access to normal feeling and normal speech.

His vigilance soon spread across his days. If someone at work touched his shoulder unexpectedly, Ravi startled violently and would need several minutes to recover. A dropped binder, footsteps in the hallway, a door opening without warning could pull him instantly into scanning mode. Living in that continual state of alarm became, for Ravi, its own kind of proof that he had been permanently changed; feeling this unsafe so often persuaded him that he was no longer an ordinary, capable man but someone fundamentally broken by what had happened. That constant readiness for threat wore him down and fed his bleak conclusions about himself. He began to think, if he were not so weak, he would not have to live like this; if he were not fundamentally altered, he would not be measuring every room for exits and walls. At the same time, the very strategies he relied on kept the danger feeling immediate. Sitting with his back to the wall made him scrutinize every movement in the room. Avoiding being alone meant he never learned that solitude could pass without catastrophe. Hurting himself brought momentary release, but afterward he felt even more ashamed and more certain that he was beyond ordinary help.

By the time he sought treatment, the pattern had become his life. He was staying late at the nonprofit less often because the empty office felt unbearable, and coworkers had noticed how rigid he became in meetings if someone stood behind him. He came in after a recent evening when a noise in his apartment hallway triggered the sounds of the assault so vividly that he ended up injuring himself and then sitting awake until dawn, convinced he was losing whatever remained of his old self. What frightened him most was that this was now permanent—that he would always be outside other people, always listening, always braced. What he hoped, though he said it carefully, was not to erase what happened but to be able to be alone in a room again without feeling hunted by it.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows threat co-occurring with avoidance, safety behaviours, and self-harm, but it does not clearly state in one paragraph that Ravi’s sense of threat leads to or drives these maladaptive strategies.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette shows threat co-occurring with avoidance, safety behaviours, and self-harm, but it does not clearly state in one paragraph that Ravi’s sense of threat leads to or drives these maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."

REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not explicitly show Ravi’s negative appraisals causing or intensifying the traumatic memory within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."

  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
